newsitem.title: USA: Republicans search for strategy on disaster bill.
newsitem.headline: Republicans search for strategy on disaster bill.

text.p: Congressional Republican leaders searched Tuesday for a strategy to respond to President Clinton's veto of disaster relief, which he said should be passed again uncluttered by political riders.

At the same time, Democrats vowed to hold an all-night talkathon in hopes of forcing action on the $8.4 billion emergency money bill and Clinton appealed for disaster assistance funds in a straightforward bill.

Clinton, who visited flood-ravaged North Dakota April 22, told a Rose Garden ceremony on education standards: "It has been 80 days since I forwarded to Congress my request for disaster relief to allow the process of recovery to begin.

"Instead of giving me a disaster relief bill, the congressional majority insisted on weighing it down on a political wish list. In the name of the people who had to face the floods, in the name of the people who need their help now, I ask the majority to put aside the political game, to set aside the political wish list," he said.

He vetoed the bill Monday because it contained unacceptable provisions about the federal budget and the census unrelated to disaster relief. Republicans insisted they were amazed he carried out his well-publicised threat to veto the bill if it arrived with the controversial provisions.
One top Senate Republican, Appropriations Committee Chairman Ted Stevens of Alaska, said he did not yet know what would happen next. "We are trying to find a strategy."

At least one senior Republican said it was time to negotiate with the White House. "They've got the political leverage. They think they are winning the PR (public relations) battle, and perhaps they are," Sen. John McCain of Arizona said.

Democrats drew unfavourable comparisons to the 1995 government shutdowns, which proved a political fiasco for Republicans whose shutdown strategy failed to force Clinton to accept their political agenda on the year's spending bills.

Republicans were to discuss their next course of action at a luncheon meeting. House Republican Leader Dick Armey said they had not decided the next step but he hoped it would be resolved this week. He said he would consider a suggestion by Republican Sen. Rod Grams of Minnesota that the offending provisions be voted on in separate legislation.

The bill provided $5.4 billion for disaster assistance in 32 states plus North and South Dakota and Minnesota, which were reeling from the worst floods of the century. Among the states that would benefit are House Speaker Newt Gingrich's home state of Georgia with $89 million and Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott's Mississippi with $24 million.

The bill also would provide $1.9 billion to pay for military operations in Bosnia and the Persian Gulf and $262 million for feeding poor women and their children, for education and for a new transportation system at Yosemite National Park. The rest of the money was earmarked for highway construction, veteran's benefits and other purposes.

What raised Democratic ire was a Republican rider to guarantee federal agencies funding at the 1997 level if the Republican-led Congress and the Democratic White House failed to agree on funding by the Oct. 1 start of the fiscal year.
The White House and congressional Democrats regarded this as a backdoor strategem that would enable Republicans to prevail in spending disputes.

Another provision Clinton refused to accept would block the use of sampling to try to get a better fix on traditionally undercounted minorities in the 2000 census. Since minorities tend to vote Democratic and congressional districts are drawn by population, this also has partisan implications.
